notes.h: Logic, quantifiers and methods of proof
notes.body:
Propositional logic. Statements are built up with ¬ (not), ∧ (and), ∨ (or), ⇒ (implies) and ⇔ (if and only if). The implication P ⇒ Q is false only when P is true and Q is false. It is logically equivalent to its contrapositive ¬Q ⇒ ¬P, but not to its converse Q ⇒ P. De Morgan's laws state that ¬(P ∧ Q) ≡ ¬P ∨ ¬Q and ¬(P ∨ Q) ≡ ¬P ∧ ¬Q.

Quantifiers. To negate a quantified statement, swap each quantifier and negate the inside: ¬(∀x P(x)) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x). Order matters. '∀ε > 0 ∃N such that ∀n ≥ N, |aₙ − L| < ε' defines aₙ → L. Its negation is '∃ε > 0 such that ∀N ∃n ≥ N with |aₙ − L| ≥ ε'. Swapping ∀x∃y to ∃y∀x gives a claim that is at least as strong, and usually strictly stronger, as in the difference between continuity and uniform continuity.

Methods of proof:
- Direct: assume P and deduce Q.
- Contrapositive: assume ¬Q and deduce ¬P. For example, if n² is even then n is even, because odd n gives odd n².
- Contradiction: assume the negation and derive a falsehood. Euclid showed there are infinitely many primes: if p₁, …, p_k were all of them, then p₁⋯p_k + 1 would have a prime factor not on the list. Similarly √2 is irrational: write √2 = a/b in lowest terms, then a² = 2b², so a is even, so b is even, a contradiction.
- Induction: if P(1) holds and P(n) ⇒ P(n + 1) for all n, then P(n) holds for all n ≥ 1. Strong induction assumes P(1), …, P(n) to prove P(n + 1). Both are equivalent to the well-ordering principle: every non-empty set of positive integers has a least element.
- Counterexample: a single case disproves a universal claim.
- Pigeonhole: if n + 1 objects go into n boxes, some box holds at least two.

Worked example. Prove that 6 | n³ − n for all n ≥ 1. The base case is 1 − 1 = 0. For the step, (n + 1)³ − (n + 1) = (n³ − n) + 3n(n + 1). The first term is divisible by 6 by hypothesis, and 3n(n + 1) is divisible by 6 because n(n + 1) is even.

Common pitfalls:
- proving the converse instead of the statement
- skipping or misplacing the base case. In the 'all horses are the same colour' fallacy, the step from n = 1 to n = 2 fails.
- negating quantifiers in the wrong order
- using examples as proof of a universal statement
- assuming what is to be proved, which is circular

Sets. The power set P(A) is the set of all subsets of A, and has 2ⁿ elements when |A| = n. To prove that two sets are equal, show inclusion both ways.

Functions. A function f: A → B assigns to each element of A exactly one element of B.
- Injective: f(a) = f(a′) ⇒ a = a′.
- Surjective: every b ∈ B equals f(a) for some a.
- Bijective: both injective and surjective. f is bijective if and only if it has a two-sided inverse.
- Composition: if f and g are injective (or surjective), so is g ∘ f. Conversely, if g ∘ f is injective then f is injective, and if g ∘ f is surjective then g is surjective.
- Images: f(A₁ ∩ A₂) ⊆ f(A₁) ∩ f(A₂), with equality for every A₁, A₂ if and only if f is injective. Preimages preserve all set operations.

Relations. A relation ~ on A is an equivalence relation if it is reflexive, symmetric and transitive. The equivalence classes partition A, and conversely every partition defines an equivalence relation. Examples:
- congruence modulo n on ℤ, with n classes
- (a, b) ~ (c, d) if and only if ad = bc on ℤ × (ℤ \ {0}), whose classes are the rational numbers
A partial order is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive, such as divisibility on ℕ.

Well-defined maps. A function defined on equivalence classes through a representative must give the same answer for every representative. For example, [a]ₙ ↦ [a]ₘ is well defined from ℤₙ to ℤₘ only when m | n.

Cardinality. |A| = |B| means there is a bijection between A and B. A set is countable if it is finite or in bijection with ℕ.
- ℤ, ℚ and ℕ × ℕ are countable.
- ℝ is uncountable, by Cantor's diagonal argument (1891).
- Cantor's theorem: there is no surjection A → P(A). If f were one, the set D = {a : a ∉ f(a)} could not be f(a) for any a.
- Schröder–Bernstein: if there are injections A → B and B → A, then |A| = |B|.

Worked example. f: ℤ → ℤ, f(n) = 2n + 1, is injective because 2n + 1 = 2m + 1 gives n = m. It is not surjective, because 2 is never a value.

Common pitfalls:
- confusing the codomain with the image
- forgetting to check that a map on classes is well defined
- thinking that an infinite proper subset must be smaller (ℕ and the even numbers have the same cardinality)

notes.h: Divisibility, congruences and the classical theorems
notes.body:
Division algorithm. For integers a and b > 0 there are unique integers q and r with a = qb + r and 0 ≤ r < b. Euclid's algorithm repeats this until the remainder is 0, and the last non-zero remainder is gcd(a, b). Working backwards gives Bézout's identity: gcd(a, b) = ax + by for some integers x and y. In particular, a and b are coprime exactly when ax + by = 1 has a solution.

Primes:
- Euclid's lemma: if p is prime and p | ab, then p | a or p | b. It follows from Bézout.
- The fundamental theorem of arithmetic: every n ≥ 2 is a product of primes, uniquely up to order. Existence comes from strong induction, uniqueness from Euclid's lemma.

Congruences. a ≡ b (mod n) means n | a − b. Congruence respects addition and multiplication.
- [a] has a multiplicative inverse in ℤₙ exactly when gcd(a, n) = 1. Find it with the extended Euclidean algorithm.
- The linear congruence ax ≡ b (mod n) is solvable exactly when d = gcd(a, n) divides b. It then has d solutions modulo n.
- Chinese remainder theorem: if m and n are coprime, the system x ≡ a (mod m), x ≡ b (mod n) has a unique solution modulo mn. Equivalently, ℤ_{mn} ≅ ℤₘ × ℤₙ.

Classical theorems:
- Fermat's little theorem: if p is prime and p ∤ a, then a^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod p).
- Euler's theorem: if gcd(a, n) = 1, then a^φ(n) ≡ 1 (mod n), where φ(n) counts the integers in 1, …, n coprime to n. φ is multiplicative, and φ(pᵏ) = pᵏ − pᵏ⁻¹.
- Wilson's theorem: (p − 1)! ≡ −1 (mod p) for p prime.
- RSA: choose n = pq and e coprime to φ(n), and compute d ≡ e⁻¹ (mod φ(n)). Encrypt with m ↦ mᵉ mod n and decrypt with c ↦ cᵈ mod n.

Worked example. gcd(252, 198): 252 = 1·198 + 54, 198 = 3·54 + 36, 54 = 1·36 + 18 and 36 = 2·18, so the gcd is 18. Back-substituting gives 18 = 54 − 36 = 4·54 − 198 = 4·252 − 5·198.

Similarly, 3^100 ≡ 3⁴ = 81 ≡ 4 (mod 7), since 3⁶ ≡ 1 by Fermat and 100 = 6·16 + 4.

Common pitfalls:
- dividing both sides of a congruence by a number that is not coprime to the modulus
- applying Fermat's theorem when p | a
- using Fermat's theorem modulo a composite number instead of Euler's
- giving one integer when the solution is a residue class

A group is a set G with a binary operation that is closed and associative, has an identity e, and gives every element an inverse. An abelian group also satisfies ab = ba. Consequences of the axioms:
- the identity and inverses are unique
- (ab)⁻¹ = b⁻¹a⁻¹
- cancellation: ab = ac ⇒ b = c
- in a finite group's Cayley table, every element appears exactly once in each row and each column

Standard examples:
- (ℤ, +), (ℚ, +), (ℝ \ {0}, ×)
- ℤₙ under addition modulo n
- U(n) = (ℤₙ)ˣ, the residues coprime to n under multiplication, of order φ(n)
- GLₙ(ℝ), the invertible n × n matrices, which is non-abelian for n ≥ 2
- the dihedral group D_n of symmetries of a regular n-gon, of order 2n. It is generated by a rotation r and a reflection s with rⁿ = s² = e and srs = r⁻¹.
- the symmetric group S_n, of order n!
- the quaternion group Q₈
Non-examples: (ℤ, −) is not associative, and (ℤ \ {0}, ×) has no inverse for 2.

Order. The order of g is the least n ≥ 1 with gⁿ = e, or infinity if there is none. Key facts:
- gᵏ = e if and only if ord(g) | k
- ord(gᵏ) = ord(g)/gcd(k, ord(g))
- in ℤₙ, the order of a is n/gcd(a, n)
- if g and h commute and have coprime orders, then ord(gh) = ord(g)ord(h)

Cyclic groups. G = ⟨g⟩ is cyclic if one element generates it. Every cyclic group is isomorphic to ℤ or to some ℤₙ. Every cyclic group is abelian, but not every abelian group is cyclic: the Klein four-group V₄ ≅ ℤ₂ × ℤ₂ is abelian but not cyclic. ℤₘ × ℤₙ is cyclic exactly when gcd(m, n) = 1. U(n) is cyclic exactly when n = 1, 2, 4, pᵏ or 2pᵏ for an odd prime p.

Worked example. U(15) = {1, 2, 4, 7, 8, 11, 13, 14}. The elements 2, 7, 8 and 13 have order 4, and 4, 11 and 14 have order 2. No element has order 8, so U(15) is not cyclic. In fact U(15) ≅ ℤ₂ × ℤ₄.

Isomorphism invariants: order, being abelian or cyclic, and the number of elements of each order. Use these to show that two groups are not isomorphic.

Common pitfalls:
- forgetting to check associativity or closure
- assuming ab = ba in general
- treating 'same order' as enough for isomorphism (ℤ₄ and V₄ both have order 4)
- writing (ab)⁻¹ = a⁻¹b⁻¹

Subgroups. H ⊆ G is a subgroup, written H ≤ G, if it is a group under the operation of G. The one-step test: H is non-empty and a, b ∈ H ⇒ ab⁻¹ ∈ H. For a finite non-empty H, closure alone is enough.

Examples of subgroups:
- the cyclic subgroup ⟨g⟩ = {gᵏ}
- the centre Z(G) = {z : zg = gz for all g}
- intersections of subgroups. Unions are usually not subgroups: H ∪ K is a subgroup only if H ⊆ K or K ⊆ H.
- the subgroups of ℤ are exactly the sets nℤ
- a cyclic group of order n has exactly one subgroup of each order dividing n

Cosets. For H ≤ G, the left coset of g is gH = {gh : h ∈ H}. Two cosets are either equal or disjoint, and aH = bH if and only if a⁻¹b ∈ H. Each coset has |H| elements, because h ↦ gh is a bijection. So the left cosets partition G into pieces of equal size. The number of cosets is the index [G : H]. Left and right cosets can differ.

Lagrange's theorem. If G is finite and H ≤ G, then |H| divides |G|, and [G : H] = |G|/|H|. Corollaries:
- ord(g) divides |G|, so g^|G| = e
- a group of prime order p is cyclic, generated by any non-identity element
- Euler's theorem follows by applying Lagrange to U(n), and Fermat's little theorem is the case n = p

The converse is false. A₄ has order 12 but no subgroup of order 6. Partial converses do exist. Cauchy's theorem says that if a prime p divides |G|, then G has an element of order p. Sylow's theorems give subgroups of every prime-power order dividing |G|.

Worked example. In S₃, let H = {e, (1 2)}. The left cosets are H, (1 3)H = {(1 3), (1 2 3)} and (2 3)H = {(2 3), (1 3 2)}. But H(1 3) = {(1 3), (1 3 2)}, so (1 3)H ≠ H(1 3). Left and right cosets differ, so H is not normal.

Common pitfalls:
- thinking a subgroup exists for every divisor of |G|
- confusing gH = Hg with gh = hg for each h
- forgetting that only H itself, among the cosets, is a subgroup
- mixing up the composition convention when computing cosets in S_n

notes.h: Homomorphisms, normal subgroups and quotient groups
notes.body:
Homomorphisms. A map φ: G → H is a homomorphism if φ(ab) = φ(a)φ(b). It follows that φ(e) = e and φ(g⁻¹) = φ(g)⁻¹. The order of φ(g) divides the order of g. Two subgroups attached to φ:
- the kernel, ker φ = {g : φ(g) = e}
- the image, im φ, a subgroup of H
φ is injective if and only if ker φ = {e}. An isomorphism is a bijective homomorphism.

Standard examples:
- det: GLₙ(ℝ) → ℝˣ, with kernel SLₙ(ℝ)
- sgn: S_n → {±1}, with kernel A_n
- ℤ → ℤₙ, k ↦ [k], with kernel nℤ
- exp: (ℝ, +) → (ℝ_{>0}, ×), an isomorphism
- ℂˣ → ℝ_{>0}, z ↦ |z|, with kernel the circle group S¹

Normal subgroups. N ≤ G is normal, written N ⊴ G, if gNg⁻¹ = N for all g, or equivalently gN = Ng for all g.
- Kernels are always normal.
- Every subgroup of an abelian group is normal.
- Every subgroup of index 2 is normal, since the only cosets are N and G \ N.
- The centre is normal.

Quotient groups. If N ⊴ G, the cosets form a group G/N under (aN)(bN) = abN, and |G/N| = [G : N]. Normality is exactly what makes this product well defined. If a′ = an and b′ = bm, then a′b′ = ab(b⁻¹nb)m, and b⁻¹nb ∈ N.

First isomorphism theorem. If φ: G → H is a homomorphism, then G/ker φ ≅ im φ, via g ker φ ↦ φ(g). Applications:
- ℤ/nℤ ≅ ℤₙ
- S_n/A_n ≅ ℤ₂, so |A_n| = n!/2
- GLₙ/SLₙ ≅ ℝˣ
- ℂˣ/S¹ ≅ ℝ_{>0}
The second and third isomorphism theorems describe HN/N ≅ H/(H ∩ N) and (G/N)/(K/N) ≅ G/K.

Worked example. A homomorphism ℤ₁₂ → ℤ₁₈ is determined by a = φ(1), which must satisfy 12a ≡ 0 (mod 18), that is 3 | a. So there are six homomorphisms, one for each a ∈ {0, 3, 6, 9, 12, 15}. Take a = 3. The image ⟨3⟩ has order 6, so the kernel has order 2 and equals {0, 6}, and ℤ₁₂/{0, 6} ≅ ℤ₆.

Common pitfalls:
- forming G/H when H is not normal
- not checking that a map defined on cosets is well defined
- assuming that a bijection between groups is an isomorphism without checking that it preserves the operation
- confusing normality with being abelian

S_n is the group of bijections of {1, …, n}, of order n!. This deck composes right to left: στ means apply τ first, then σ. Check which convention your course uses.

Cycle notation. Every permutation is a product of disjoint cycles, uniquely up to the order of the cycles and the choice of starting point within each cycle. Disjoint cycles commute.
- The order of a permutation is the least common multiple of its cycle lengths. For example, (1 2 3)(4 5) has order 6.
- A k-cycle is a product of k − 1 transpositions: (a₁ a₂ … a_k) = (a₁ a_k)(a₁ a_{k−1})⋯(a₁ a₂). Hence the transpositions generate S_n.

Sign. The sign sgn(σ) = (−1)^(number of transpositions) is well defined. One way to see this: σ ↦ Π_{i<j}(σ(j) − σ(i))/(j − i) is a homomorphism to {±1}. Equivalently, sgn(σ) = (−1)^(n − c), where c counts the cycles, including fixed points. A k-cycle has sign (−1)^(k−1), so cycles of even length are odd permutations. The alternating group A_n = ker(sgn) has order n!/2 and is generated by 3-cycles for n ≥ 3.

Conjugacy. For any τ, τ(a₁ … a_k)τ⁻¹ = (τ(a₁) … τ(a_k)). So two permutations are conjugate in S_n exactly when they have the same cycle type. The conjugacy classes of S_n therefore correspond to partitions of n. For S₅ the class sizes are:
- identity 1
- transpositions 10
- 3-cycles 20
- 4-cycles 30
- 5-cycles 24
- double transpositions 15
- a 3-cycle times a disjoint transposition 20
These total 120.

Key theorems:
- Cayley's theorem: every group G embeds in Sym(G), through g ↦ (x ↦ gx). So every finite group is isomorphic to a subgroup of some S_n.
- A_n is simple for n ≥ 5. A₄ is not simple, since V₄ ⊴ A₄.

Worked example. Let σ ∈ S₈ map 1, 2, …, 8 to 3, 5, 1, 8, 7, 2, 4, 6 respectively. Following each element gives σ = (1 3)(2 5 7 4 8 6). Its order is lcm(2, 6) = 6. Its sign is (−1)(−1) = +1, or equivalently (−1)^(8−2) = +1. So σ is even and lies in A₈.

Common pitfalls:
- mixing composition conventions within one answer
- taking the order to be the sum or product of the cycle lengths, rather than their lcm (and the lcm rule itself applies only to disjoint cycles)
- forgetting that a 2-cycle is odd and a 3-cycle is even
- assuming that conjugacy classes in A_n are the same as in S_n. Some S_n-classes split in two.

A ring is an abelian group under +, with an associative multiplication that distributes over addition. Here rings are commutative with 1.
- A unit is an invertible element.
- A zero divisor is a ≠ 0 with ab = 0 for some b ≠ 0.
- An integral domain is a commutative ring with 1 ≠ 0 and no zero divisors.
- A field is a commutative ring with 1 ≠ 0 in which every non-zero element is a unit.
Examples:
- ℤₙ is a field exactly when n is prime (in ℤ₆, 2 · 3 = 0).
- every finite integral domain is a field, because x ↦ ax is injective and hence surjective

Ideals and quotients. An ideal I ⊴ R is an additive subgroup with rI ⊆ I for all r ∈ R. Then R/I is a ring.
- The kernel of a ring homomorphism φ is an ideal, and R/ker φ ≅ im φ.
- In a commutative ring with 1, I is prime exactly when R/I is an integral domain, and maximal exactly when R/I is a field.
- Every maximal ideal is prime. In ℤ, (0) is prime but not maximal.
- ℤ and F[x] (F a field) are principal ideal domains.

Polynomials over a field F. F[x] has a division algorithm, and deg(fg) = deg f + deg g.
- Factor theorem: (x − a) divides f exactly when f(a) = 0.
- A polynomial of degree n has at most n roots in F.
- A polynomial of degree 2 or 3 is irreducible over F exactly when it has no root in F. For degree 4 or more it fails: (x² + 1)² has no real roots.
- Eisenstein's criterion gives irreducibility over ℚ.
- F[x]/(p(x)) is a field exactly when p is irreducible. It then has q^(deg p) elements when |F| = q.

Finite fields. Every finite field has prime-power order pⁿ, and for each such order there is exactly one field up to isomorphism. Its multiplicative group is cyclic.

Worked example. x³ + x + 1 has no root in F₂, since it takes the value 1 at both 0 and 1, so it is irreducible. Then F₂[x]/(x³ + x + 1) is a field with 8 elements. With α the class of x, α³ = α + 1, and the powers of α run through 1, α, α², α + 1, α² + α, α² + α + 1, α² + 1 before returning to 1. So α generates all 7 non-zero elements.

Common pitfalls:
- applying the 'no roots means irreducible' test to degree 4 or more
- confusing a subring with an ideal

cards.f: What is the contrapositive of P ⇒ Q, and is it equivalent to P ⇒ Q?
cards.b: ¬Q ⇒ ¬P. Yes, it is logically equivalent to P ⇒ Q. The converse Q ⇒ P is not.

cards.f: Negate: ∀ε > 0 ∃δ > 0 ∀x (|x − a| < δ ⇒ |f(x) − f(a)| < ε).
cards.b: ∃ε > 0 ∀δ > 0 ∃x such that |x − a| < δ and |f(x) − f(a)| ≥ ε.

cards.f: State De Morgan's laws for propositions.
State the principle of mathematical induction.
cards.b: If P(1) is true, and P(n) ⇒ P(n + 1) for every n ≥ 1, then P(n) is true for all n ≥ 1.

cards.f: What is strong induction, and when is it useful?
cards.b: You prove P(n + 1) assuming all of P(1), …, P(n). It helps when the step depends on earlier cases, as in prime factorisation or recurrences like the Fibonacci numbers.

cards.f: State the well-ordering principle.
cards.b: Every non-empty subset of the positive integers has a least element. It is equivalent to induction.

cards.f: Outline Euclid's proof that there are infinitely many primes.
cards.b: Suppose p₁, …, p_k are all the primes. N = p₁⋯p_k + 1 leaves remainder 1 on division by each pᵢ, yet N > 1 has a prime factor, which must be a new prime. Contradiction.

cards.f: Why does the 'all horses are the same colour' induction fail?
cards.b: The step from n to n + 1 uses two overlapping groups of n horses. When n = 1 the groups do not overlap, so P(1) ⇒ P(2) fails.

cards.f: Is ∃y ∀x P(x, y) the same as ∀x ∃y P(x, y)?
cards.b: No. ∃y ∀x is stronger: one y must work for every x. For example, ∀x ∈ ℝ ∃y (y > x) is true, but ∃y ∀x (y > x) is false.

cards.f: Define injective, surjective and bijective.
cards.b: Injective: f(a) = f(a′) ⇒ a = a′. Surjective: every element of the codomain is f(a) for some a. Bijective: both.

cards.f: If g ∘ f is injective, what can you conclude about f and g?
cards.b: f must be injective. g need not be, because g only has to be injective on the image of f.

cards.f: State the three properties of an equivalence relation.
cards.b: Reflexive (a ~ a), symmetric (a ~ b ⇒ b ~ a) and transitive (a ~ b and b ~ c ⇒ a ~ c).

cards.f: How are equivalence relations and partitions related?
cards.b: The equivalence classes of a relation on A partition A. Conversely, any partition of A defines the equivalence relation 'lies in the same block'.

cards.f: Define a partial order and give an example.
cards.b: A relation that is reflexive, antisymmetric (a ≤ b and b ≤ a ⇒ a = b) and transitive. For example, divisibility on ℕ.

cards.f: When is f(A₁ ∩ A₂) = f(A₁) ∩ f(A₂) for all subsets A₁, A₂?
cards.b: Exactly when f is injective. In general only ⊆ holds.

cards.f: State Cantor's theorem.
cards.b: For any set A, there is no surjection A → P(A). So |A| < |P(A)|.

cards.f: Why is ℚ countable?
cards.b: List the positive fractions p/q by increasing p + q, skipping repeats. This gives a surjection from ℕ onto ℚ₊. Interleaving 0 and the negatives then covers ℚ.

cards.f: State the Schröder–Bernstein theorem.
cards.b: If there are injections A → B and B → A, then there is a bijection A → B.

cards.f: State Bézout's identity.
cards.b: For integers a and b, not both zero, there are integers x and y with ax + by = gcd(a, b). The gcd is the smallest positive integer of this form.

cards.f: Find gcd(252, 198) and express it as a combination of 252 and 198.
cards.b: gcd = 18, and 18 = 4·252 − 5·198, from Euclid's algorithm and back-substitution.

cards.f: When does ax ≡ b (mod n) have a solution, and how many solutions are there?
cards.b: Exactly when d = gcd(a, n) divides b. There are then d solutions modulo n.

cards.f: State the Chinese remainder theorem for two moduli.
cards.b: If gcd(m, n) = 1, then x ≡ a (mod m) and x ≡ b (mod n) have a unique common solution modulo mn.

cards.f: State Fermat's little theorem.
cards.b: If p is prime and p ∤ a, then a^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod p). Equivalently, aᵖ ≡ a (mod p) for all integers a.

cards.f: State Euler's theorem and the formula for φ(n).
cards.b: If gcd(a, n) = 1 then a^φ(n) ≡ 1 (mod n). If n = Π pᵢ^kᵢ, then φ(n) = n Π (1 − 1/pᵢ).

cards.f: State Wilson's theorem.
cards.b: An integer p > 1 is prime if and only if (p − 1)! ≡ −1 (mod p).

cards.f: Compute 2^1000 mod 13.
Why does RSA decryption recover the message (when gcd(m, n) = 1)?
cards.b: ed = 1 + kφ(n), so (mᵉ)ᵈ = m(m^φ(n))ᵏ ≡ m (mod n) by Euler's theorem. The general case follows from the CRT modulo p and q.

cards.f: List the group axioms.
cards.b: Closure, associativity, an identity element e, and an inverse for every element.

cards.f: Why is (ℤ, −) not a group?
cards.b: Subtraction is not associative: (1 − 2) − 3 = −4 but 1 − (2 − 3) = 2. It also has no two-sided identity.

cards.f: What is the order of a in ℤₙ?
cards.b: n/gcd(a, n). For example, 6 has order 15/3 = 5 in ℤ₁₅.

cards.f: State the order and the defining relations of the dihedral group D_n.
cards.b: |D_n| = 2n, with generators r (a rotation) and s (a reflection) satisfying rⁿ = s² = e and srs = r⁻¹.

cards.f: When is ℤₘ × ℤₙ cyclic?
cards.b: Exactly when gcd(m, n) = 1. Then it is isomorphic to ℤ_{mn}.

cards.f: Is every abelian group cyclic?
cards.b: No. The Klein four-group ℤ₂ × ℤ₂ is abelian, but every non-identity element has order 2, so none generates it.

cards.f: If gᵏ = e, what can you say about ord(g)?
cards.b: ord(g) divides k. Write k = q·ord(g) + r with 0 ≤ r < ord(g); then gʳ = e, so r = 0.

cards.f: Give a formula for ord(gᵏ) when g has finite order n.
cards.b: ord(gᵏ) = n/gcd(n, k).

cards.f: Is U(15) cyclic?
cards.b: No. Its elements have orders 1, 2 or 4, so none has order 8. In fact U(15) ≅ ℤ₂ × ℤ₄.

cards.f: State the one-step subgroup test.
cards.b: A subset H of G is a subgroup if and only if H is non-empty and ab⁻¹ ∈ H whenever a, b ∈ H.

cards.f: State Lagrange's theorem.
cards.b: If G is finite and H ≤ G, then |H| divides |G|, and the number of cosets is [G : H] = |G|/|H|.

cards.f: When are two left cosets aH and bH equal?
cards.b: Exactly when a⁻¹b ∈ H. Otherwise they are disjoint.

cards.f: Why is a group of prime order cyclic?
cards.b: Take any g ≠ e. By Lagrange, ord(g) divides p and is not 1, so it equals p, and ⟨g⟩ = G.

cards.f: Is the converse of Lagrange's theorem true?
cards.b: No. A₄ has order 12 but no subgroup of order 6.

cards.f: State Cauchy's theorem.
cards.b: If a prime p divides |G|, then G contains an element of order p.

cards.f: How does Euler's theorem follow from Lagrange?
cards.b: U(n) is a group of order φ(n). The order of a divides φ(n), so a^φ(n) = 1 in U(n).

cards.f: When is the union of two subgroups a subgroup?
cards.b: Only when one contains the other. Otherwise pick h ∈ H \ K and k ∈ K \ H; then hk lies in neither.

cards.f: What are the subgroups of a cyclic group of order n?
cards.b: Exactly one subgroup of order d for each divisor d of n, namely ⟨g^(n/d)⟩. Each is cyclic.

cards.f: Define the kernel of a homomorphism, and state when the homomorphism is injective.
cards.b: ker φ = {g ∈ G : φ(g) = e_H}. φ is injective if and only if ker φ = {e}.

cards.f: Define a normal subgroup.
cards.b: N ≤ G is normal if gNg⁻¹ = N for every g in G, or equivalently if every left coset gN equals the right coset Ng.

cards.f: Why is every subgroup of index 2 normal?
cards.b: The two left cosets are H and G \ H, and so are the two right cosets. So gH = Hg for every g.

cards.f: State the first isomorphism theorem for groups.
cards.b: If φ: G → H is a homomorphism, then ker φ ⊴ G and G/ker φ ≅ im φ, via g ker φ ↦ φ(g).

cards.f: Why must N be normal for G/N to be a group?
cards.b: The product (aN)(bN) = abN must not depend on the representatives. This holds exactly when b⁻¹Nb ⊆ N for all b, which is normality.

cards.f: Apply the first isomorphism theorem to det on GLₙ(ℝ).
cards.b: det is a surjective homomorphism onto ℝˣ with kernel SLₙ(ℝ), so GLₙ(ℝ)/SLₙ(ℝ) ≅ ℝˣ.

cards.f: How many homomorphisms are there from ℤₘ to ℤₙ?
cards.b: gcd(m, n). The homomorphism is fixed by φ(1) = a, which needs ma ≡ 0 (mod n).

cards.f: Give a bijection between groups of the same order that is not an isomorphism.
cards.b: Any bijection ℤ₄ → ℤ₂ × ℤ₂. An isomorphism must preserve orders, but ℤ₄ has an element of order 4 and ℤ₂ × ℤ₂ does not.

cards.f: What is the kernel of z ↦ |z| from ℂˣ to ℝ_{>0}, and what does the first isomorphism theorem give?
cards.b: The kernel is the circle group S¹ = {z : |z| = 1}. The map is surjective, so ℂˣ/S¹ ≅ ℝ_{>0}.

cards.f: How do you find the order of a permutation from its disjoint cycle decomposition?
cards.b: Take the lcm of the cycle lengths. For example, (1 2 3)(4 5) has order 6.

cards.f: What is the sign of a k-cycle?
cards.b: (−1)^(k−1). It is a product of k − 1 transpositions, so a 3-cycle is even and a 4-cycle is odd.

cards.f: Write (1 2 3 4) as a product of transpositions (composing right to left).
cards.b: (1 4)(1 3)(1 2). There are three transpositions, so it is odd.

cards.f: When are two permutations conjugate in S_n?
cards.b: Exactly when they have the same cycle type, because τ(a₁ … a_k)τ⁻¹ = (τ(a₁) … τ(a_k)).

cards.f: How many 3-cycles are there in S₅?
cards.b: C(5,3) × 2 = 20. Each 3-element subset gives two distinct 3-cycles.

cards.f: State Cayley's theorem.
cards.b: Every group G is isomorphic to a subgroup of Sym(G), via g ↦ (x ↦ gx). A group of order n embeds in S_n.

cards.f: What is the order of A_n, and what generates it?
cards.b: n!/2. For n ≥ 3 it is generated by the 3-cycles.

cards.f: What is the largest order of an element of S₇?
cards.b: 12, from cycle type (3, 4). Other partitions of 7 give lcm at most 10, for example (2, 5).

cards.f: Write the permutation of {1, …, 8} sending 1, …, 8 to 3, 5, 1, 8, 7, 2, 4, 6 in cycles, and give its order and sign.
cards.b: (1 3)(2 5 7 4 8 6). Its order is lcm(2, 6) = 6, and its sign is (−1)(−1) = +1, so it is even.

cards.f: Define an integral domain.
cards.b: A commutative ring with 1 ≠ 0 and no zero divisors: ab = 0 ⇒ a = 0 or b = 0.

cards.f: For which n is ℤₙ a field?
cards.b: Exactly when n is prime. If n = ab with 1 < a, b < n, then a and b are zero divisors.

cards.f: Why is every finite integral domain a field?
cards.b: For a ≠ 0, the map x ↦ ax is injective by cancellation, hence surjective because the ring is finite. So ax = 1 for some x.

cards.f: Define an ideal.
cards.b: An additive subgroup I of R with ra ∈ I and ar ∈ I for all r ∈ R and a ∈ I.

cards.f: Relate prime and maximal ideals to quotient rings.
cards.b: In a commutative ring with 1, I is prime exactly when R/I is an integral domain, and maximal exactly when R/I is a field.

cards.f: When is a cubic irreducible over a field F?
cards.b: Exactly when it has no root in F, since any factorisation would include a linear factor. This test fails for degree 4 or more.

cards.f: State Eisenstein's criterion.
cards.b: If, for some prime p, p divides every coefficient of f ∈ ℤ[x] except the leading one, p does not divide the leading coefficient, and p² does not divide the constant term, then f is irreducible over ℚ.

cards.f: When is F[x]/(p(x)) a field?
cards.b: Exactly when p(x) is irreducible over F. If |F| = q and deg p = n, the field has qⁿ elements.

cards.f: In F₂[x]/(x³ + x + 1), with α the class of x, find α⁻¹.
cards.b: α³ = α + 1, so α(α² + 1) = α³ + α = 1 (characteristic 2). Hence α⁻¹ = α² + 1.

questions.q: What is the contrapositive of 'If n² is odd, then n is odd'?
options: If n is even, then n² is even
If n is odd, then n² is odd
If n² is even, then n is even
If n is even, then n² is odd
questions.why: The contrapositive of P ⇒ Q is ¬Q ⇒ ¬P. Here that is 'n not odd ⇒ n² not odd', which says that if n is even then n² is even. Option B is the converse.

questions.q: Which statement is the negation of 'aₙ → L', that is, of ∀ε > 0 ∃N ∀n ≥ N: |aₙ − L| < ε?
options: ∃ε > 0 ∀N ∃n ≥ N: |aₙ − L| ≥ ε
∀ε > 0 ∃N ∀n ≥ N: |aₙ − L| ≥ ε
∃ε > 0 ∃N ∀n ≥ N: |aₙ − L| ≥ ε
∀ε > 0 ∀N ∃n ≥ N: |aₙ − L| ≥ ε
questions.why: Each quantifier is swapped (∀ ↔ ∃) and the final inequality is negated. So some ε is exceeded infinitely often, beyond every N.

questions.q: Prove that √2 is irrational.
markScheme: Assumes for contradiction that √2 = a/b with integers a, b, b ≠ 0, in lowest terms
Squares to get a² = 2b², so a² is even, so a is even (by the contrapositive of 'a odd ⇒ a² odd')
Writes a = 2k, so 4k² = 2b², b² = 2k², so b is even
Contradiction with lowest terms, so √2 is irrational
questions.modelAnswer: Suppose for contradiction that √2 = a/b, where a and b are integers, b ≠ 0, and gcd(a, b) = 1. Then a² = 2b², so a² is even. If a were odd, a² would be odd, so a is even. Write a = 2k. Then 4k² = 2b², so b² = 2k², and by the same argument b is even. So 2 divides both a and b, contradicting gcd(a, b) = 1. Hence √2 is irrational.

questions.q:
(a) Prove by induction that 6 divides n³ − n for every integer n ≥ 1. [4]
(b) Prove by induction that 1³ + 2³ + … + n³ = (n(n + 1)/2)² for all n ≥ 1. [4]
(c) Mia argues: 'Claim: in any set of n horses, all have the same colour. It is true for n = 1. Assume it for n. Given n + 1 horses, remove the first: the remaining n share a colour. Remove the last instead: those n share a colour. The groups overlap, so all n + 1 share a colour.' Identify precisely where the argument fails. [4]
markScheme: (a) Base case: 1 − 1 = 0, which is divisible by 6
(a) Expands (n + 1)³ − (n + 1) = (n³ − n) + 3n(n + 1)
(a) Uses the hypothesis and the fact that n(n + 1) is even, so 6 | 3n(n + 1)
(b) Base case 1 = 1²
(b) Adds (n + 1)³ to n²(n + 1)²/4 and factorises to (n + 1)²(n² + 4n + 4)/4 = ((n + 1)(n + 2)/2)²
(c) Notes that the inductive step must hold for every n ≥ 1, including n = 1
(c) For n = 1 (two horses), the two groups of size 1 do not overlap
(c) So P(1) ⇒ P(2) fails, and the chain of implications breaks at the first link
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Let P(n) be the statement 6 | n³ − n. P(1) holds since 1 − 1 = 0. Assume P(n). Then (n + 1)³ − (n + 1) = n³ + 3n² + 3n + 1 − n − 1 = (n³ − n) + 3n(n + 1). By hypothesis 6 | n³ − n. One of n and n + 1 is even, so 2 | n(n + 1) and 6 | 3n(n + 1). Hence 6 divides the sum, so P(n + 1) holds, and by induction P(n) holds for all n ≥ 1. A direct proof is also possible, since n³ − n = (n − 1)n(n + 1) is a product of three consecutive integers.

(b) For n = 1 both sides equal 1. Assume the formula for n. Then Σ_{k=1}^{n+1} k³ = n²(n + 1)²/4 + (n + 1)³ = (n + 1)²(n² + 4n + 4)/4 = (n + 1)²(n + 2)²/4, which is the formula for n + 1. By induction it holds for all n ≥ 1.

(c) An inductive step must prove P(n) ⇒ P(n + 1) for every n ≥ 1, using an argument valid for each n. Mia's argument uses the fact that the two groups of n horses share at least one horse, so that the colours can be linked. With n + 1 horses the groups share n − 1 horses, and that is zero when n = 1. With two horses, removing the first leaves {horse 2} and removing the last leaves {horse 1}. Each group is trivially one colour, but nothing links the two. So P(1) ⇒ P(2) is not proved, and since every later case depends on it, the conclusion does not follow. The steps P(n) ⇒ P(n + 1) for n ≥ 2 are valid, but they are useless without P(2).

questions.q: Define f: ℤ → ℤ by f(n) = 2n + 1. Which is true?
options: f is injective but not surjective
f is surjective but not injective
f is bijective
f is neither injective nor surjective
questions.why: 2n + 1 = 2m + 1 gives n = m, so f is injective. Every value is odd, so even integers such as 2 are never hit, and f is not surjective.

questions.q: Let f: A → B and g: B → C be functions. Prove that (i) if f and g are injective then g ∘ f is injective, and (ii) if g ∘ f is injective then f is injective. Give an example showing that g need not be injective in (ii).
markScheme: (i) g(f(a)) = g(f(a′)) ⇒ f(a) = f(a′) by injectivity of g ⇒ a = a′ by injectivity of f
Example: A = {1}, B = {1, 2}, C = {1}, with f(1) = 1 and g constant
Checks that g ∘ f is injective but g is not
questions.modelAnswer: (i) Suppose g(f(a)) = g(f(a′)). Since g is injective, f(a) = f(a′). Since f is injective, a = a′. (ii) Suppose f(a) = f(a′). Applying g gives (g ∘ f)(a) = (g ∘ f)(a′), and injectivity of g ∘ f gives a = a′. For the example, let A = {1}, B = {1, 2} and C = {1}, with f(1) = 1 and g(1) = g(2) = 1. Then g ∘ f is injective because its domain has one point, but g is not injective.

questions.q:
Define a relation on ℝ by x ~ y if and only if x − y ∈ ℤ.
(a) Prove that ~ is an equivalence relation. [3]
(b) Describe the equivalence classes, and give a set containing exactly one element from each class. [1]
(c) Decide whether F([x]) = cos(2πx) and G([x]) = x² give well-defined functions on the set of classes. [2]
markScheme: Reflexive: x − x = 0 ∈ ℤ
Symmetric: x − y ∈ ℤ ⇒ y − x = −(x − y) ∈ ℤ
Transitive: (x − y) + (y − z) = x − z ∈ ℤ
Classes are x + ℤ; the set [0, 1) contains exactly one representative of each
F is well defined, since cos is 2π-periodic so cos(2π(x + n)) = cos(2πx)
G is not well defined: 0 ~ 1 but 0² ≠ 1²
questions.modelAnswer: (a) For reflexivity, x − x = 0 ∈ ℤ. For symmetry, if x − y ∈ ℤ then y − x = −(x − y) ∈ ℤ. For transitivity, if x − y and y − z are integers, so is their sum x − z. (b) The class of x is x + ℤ = {x + n : n ∈ ℤ}. Each class meets [0, 1) in exactly one point, the fractional part of x. (c) F is well defined: if x ~ y then y = x + n, and cos(2π(x + n)) = cos(2πx). G is not well defined, because 0 ~ 1 but 0² = 0 ≠ 1 = 1².

questions.q:
(a) Prove that ℕ × ℕ is countable, and deduce that ℚ is countable. [6]
(b) Prove, using Cantor's diagonal argument, that the interval (0, 1) is uncountable. Address the issue of non-unique decimal expansions. [6]
(c) Prove Cantor's theorem: for any set A there is no surjection A → P(A). [5]
(d) Deduce that there is no 'largest' cardinality. [3]
markScheme: (a) Gives an explicit bijection or injection, e.g. (m, n) ↦ 2ᵐ3ⁿ is injective by unique factorisation, or the diagonal enumeration
(a) Maps ℚ₊ injectively into ℕ × ℕ via p/q in lowest terms ↦ (p, q), then handles 0 and the negatives
(b) Assumes a list x₁, x₂, … of all reals in (0, 1) with decimal expansions, choosing expansions that do not end in recurring 9s
(b) Defines y with nth digit 5 if the nth digit of xₙ is not 5, and 4 otherwise
(b) y ∈ (0, 1) has a unique expansion (no 0s or 9s), and differs from each xₙ in the nth digit, a contradiction
(c) Supposes f: A → P(A) is surjective and defines D = {a ∈ A : a ∉ f(a)}
(c) If D = f(d), then d ∈ D ⇔ d ∉ f(d) = D, a contradiction
(d) For any set A, P(A) has strictly greater cardinality, since a ↦ {a} injects A into P(A) and there is no bijection
(d) Iterating gives an unending chain |A| < |P(A)| < |P(P(A))| < …
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The map (m, n) ↦ 2ᵐ3ⁿ from ℕ × ℕ to ℕ is injective by the fundamental theorem of arithmetic, so ℕ × ℕ is in bijection with an infinite subset of ℕ and is therefore countable. Alternatively, list the pairs along the diagonals m + n = constant. Each positive rational has a unique lowest-terms form p/q, and p/q ↦ (p, q) injects ℚ₊ into ℕ × ℕ, so ℚ₊ is countable. Then ℚ = ℚ₊ ∪ {0} ∪ (−ℚ₊) is a finite union of countable sets, listed by interleaving: 0, q₁, −q₁, q₂, −q₂, ….

(b) Every x ∈ (0, 1) has a decimal expansion 0.d₁d₂d₃…, unique if we forbid expansions ending in recurring 9s. Suppose x₁, x₂, … lists all of (0, 1), and let dₙₙ be the nth digit of xₙ. Define y = 0.e₁e₂… with eₙ = 5 if dₙₙ ≠ 5, and eₙ = 4 if dₙₙ = 5. Then y ∈ (0, 1), and its expansion contains no 0s or 9s, so it is the unique expansion of y. y differs from xₙ in the nth digit, so y ≠ xₙ for every n, contradicting the assumption that the list was complete. Hence (0, 1), and so ℝ, is uncountable.

(c) Suppose f: A → P(A) is surjective. Let D = {a ∈ A : a ∉ f(a)} ∈ P(A). By surjectivity D = f(d) for some d. If d ∈ D, then by definition d ∉ f(d) = D. If d ∉ D = f(d), then d satisfies the defining condition, so d ∈ D. Either way there is a contradiction, so no surjection exists.

(d) The map a ↦ {a} injects A into P(A), so |A| ≤ |P(A)|. By (c) there is no bijection, so |A| < |P(A)|. Whatever set we start with, its power set is strictly larger, giving an infinite ascending chain |ℕ| < |P(ℕ)| < |P(P(ℕ))| < ….

questions.q: What is 3^100 mod 7?
Use Euclid's algorithm to find gcd(252, 198), and find integers x and y with 252x + 198y = gcd(252, 198).
Solve the congruence 17x ≡ 5 (mod 43).
markScheme: Notes gcd(17, 43) = 1, so there is a unique solution modulo 43
Back-substitution gives 1 = 2·43 − 5·17, so 17⁻¹ ≡ −5 ≡ 38 (mod 43)
questions.modelAnswer: Since 43 is prime and does not divide 17, the solution is unique modulo 43. Euclid's algorithm gives 43 = 2·17 + 9, 17 = 9 + 8 and 9 = 8 + 1. Back-substituting, 1 = 9 − 8 = 9 − (17 − 9) = 2·9 − 17 = 2(43 − 2·17) − 17 = 2·43 − 5·17. So 17⁻¹ ≡ −5 ≡ 38 (mod 43). Then x ≡ 38·5 = 190 = 4·43 + 18, so x ≡ 18 (mod 43). Check: 17·18 = 306 = 301 + 5.

questions.q:
Amira is packing sweets for a school fair. When she packs them in bags of 3, two are left over; in bags of 5, three are left over; in bags of 7, two are left over. She knows she has fewer than 200 sweets.
(a) Write the information as a system of congruences, and explain why the Chinese remainder theorem guarantees a unique solution modulo 105. [3]
(b) Solve the system, showing your method. [6]
(c) List every possible number of sweets. [1]
(d) Prove the uniqueness part of the CRT for two coprime moduli m and n. [2]
markScheme: (a) x ≡ 2 (mod 3), x ≡ 3 (mod 5), x ≡ 2 (mod 7)
(a) The moduli are pairwise coprime, with product 105
(b) Combines x ≡ 2 (mod 3) and x ≡ 2 (mod 7) to get x ≡ 2 (mod 21)
(b) Writes x = 2 + 21k and needs 2 + 21k ≡ 3 (mod 5), i.e. k ≡ 1 (mod 5)
(b) General solution x ≡ 23 (mod 105)
(c) 23 and 128 (the next, 233, exceeds 200)
(d) If x and y both solve the system, then m | x − y and n | x − y, so mn | x − y since gcd(m, n) = 1
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Let x be the number of sweets. Then x ≡ 2 (mod 3), x ≡ 3 (mod 5) and x ≡ 2 (mod 7). The moduli 3, 5 and 7 are pairwise coprime, so by the Chinese remainder theorem the system has exactly one solution modulo 3·5·7 = 105.

(b) The first and third congruences both say x ≡ 2. Since 3 and 7 are coprime, they combine to x ≡ 2 (mod 21). Write x = 2 + 21k. The remaining condition is 2 + 21k ≡ 3 (mod 5). Since 21 ≡ 1 (mod 5), this becomes k ≡ 1 (mod 5), so k = 1 + 5j and x = 2 + 21(1 + 5j) = 23 + 105j. Check: 23 = 3·7 + 2, 23 = 5·4 + 3, 23 = 7·3 + 2. So x ≡ 23 (mod 105).

The general constructive method gives the same answer. With N = 105 and partial products 35, 21 and 15, we find inverses: 35 ≡ 2 (mod 3) has inverse 2, 21 ≡ 1 (mod 5) has inverse 1, and 15 ≡ 1 (mod 7) has inverse 1. Then x ≡ 2·35·2 + 3·21·1 + 2·15·1 = 140 + 63 + 30 = 233 ≡ 23 (mod 105).

(c) The positive solutions below 200 are 23 and 128. The next one, 233, is too large. So Amira has either 23 or 128 sweets, and one more piece of information, such as a rough estimate, would settle it.

(d) Suppose x and y both satisfy x ≡ a (mod m) and x ≡ b (mod n). Then m | x − y and n | x − y. Since gcd(m, n) = 1, Bézout gives mu + nv = 1, so x − y = (x − y)mu + (x − y)nv. Each term is divisible by mn, so x ≡ y (mod mn).

questions.q:
Bob publishes the RSA public key (n, e) = (143, 7). Alice encrypts the message m = 9 and sends c = mᵉ mod n.
(a) Compute c, showing your working with repeated squaring. [4]
(b) Given that 143 = 11 × 13, compute φ(143) and use the extended Euclidean algorithm to find Bob's private exponent d. [5]
(c) Verify that cᵈ ≡ 9 (mod 143). You may use the Chinese remainder theorem to simplify. [4]
(d) Prove that decryption works for any message m with gcd(m, n) = 1. [3]
markScheme: (c) CRT: x ≡ 9 (mod 11) and x ≡ 9 (mod 13) give x ≡ 9 (mod 143)
(d) ed = 1 + kφ(n), so c^d = m^(1 + kφ(n)) = m·(m^φ(n))ᵏ ≡ m by Euler's theorem
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) 9² = 81. Then 9⁴ ≡ 81² = 6561, and 6561 − 45·143 = 6561 − 6435 = 126, so 9⁴ ≡ 126. Then 9⁷ = 9⁴·9²·9 ≡ 126·81·9. Now 126·81 = 10206 = 71·143 + 53, so this is 53·9 = 477 = 3·143 + 48. Hence c = 48.

(b) φ(143) = (11 − 1)(13 − 1) = 120. We need d with 7d ≡ 1 (mod 120). Euclid gives 120 = 17·7 + 1, so 1 = 120 − 17·7, and d ≡ −17 ≡ 103 (mod 120). Check: 7·103 = 721 = 6·120 + 1.

(c) Rather than computing 48^103 mod 143 directly, work modulo 11 and 13. Modulo 11, 48 ≡ 4. Fermat gives 4¹⁰ ≡ 1, and 103 ≡ 3 (mod 10), so 48^103 ≡ 4³ = 64 ≡ 9 (mod 11). Modulo 13, 48 ≡ 9. Here 9³ = 729 = 56·13 + 1 ≡ 1, so 9 has order 3, and 103 ≡ 1 (mod 3), giving 48^103 ≡ 9 (mod 13). The number 9 satisfies both congruences, and by uniqueness in the CRT, 48^103 ≡ 9 (mod 143). Bob recovers Alice's message.

(d) Since ed ≡ 1 (mod φ(n)), we can write ed = 1 + kφ(n) for some integer k ≥ 0. Then cᵈ ≡ m^(ed) = m·(m^φ(n))ᵏ (mod n). If gcd(m, n) = 1, Euler's theorem gives m^φ(n) ≡ 1, so cᵈ ≡ m (mod n). Since 0 ≤ m < n, reducing modulo n returns m exactly. The case gcd(m, n) > 1 also works, by checking modulo p and q separately, but such m are vanishingly rare for realistic key sizes.

questions.q: Which of the following is a group?
questions.why: (ℤ, +) satisfies all four axioms. Subtraction is not associative, 2 has no multiplicative inverse in ℤ, and positive integers have no additive inverses in ℕ.

questions.q: What is the order of the element 6 in the additive group ℤ₁₅?
questions.why: The order of a in ℤₙ is n/gcd(a, n) = 15/3 = 5. Check: 5·6 = 30 ≡ 0, and no smaller positive multiple of 6 is divisible by 15.

questions.q: Let G be a group in which g² = e for every g ∈ G. Prove that G is abelian.
markScheme: g² = e implies g = g⁻¹ for every g
Applies this to ab: (ab)⁻¹ = ab
Uses (ab)⁻¹ = b⁻¹a⁻¹ = ba
Concludes ab = ba for all a, b
questions.modelAnswer: For every g, g² = e means g = g⁻¹. Take any a, b ∈ G. Then ab = (ab)⁻¹, since ab is also an element of G. In any group (ab)⁻¹ = b⁻¹a⁻¹, and here b⁻¹ = b and a⁻¹ = a, so (ab)⁻¹ = ba. Hence ab = ba for all a and b, so G is abelian. Examples include the Klein four-group and ℤ₂ⁿ.

questions.q:
Let U(15) be the group of residues modulo 15 that are coprime to 15, under multiplication.
(a) List the elements of U(15), and state its order. [2]
(b) Find the order of each element. [4]
(c) Prove that U(15) is not cyclic, and that it is isomorphic to ℤ₂ × ℤ₄ but not to ℤ₂ × ℤ₂ × ℤ₂. [5]
(d) Compute 7^101 mod 15. [3]
markScheme: (b) 11 and 14 have order 2 (121 ≡ 1, 196 ≡ 1); 13 has order 4
(c) No element of order 8, so U(15) is not cyclic

(c) ℤ₂ × ℤ₄ has the same order profile (one identity, three elements of order 2, four of order 4); gives an explicit isomorphism, e.g. via generators 2 (order 4) and 11 (order 2) with ⟨2⟩ ∩ ⟨11⟩ = {1}
(c) ℤ₂³ has no element of order 4, so it is not isomorphic
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The residues coprime to 15 are 1, 2, 4, 7, 8, 11, 13 and 14, so |U(15)| = φ(15) = φ(3)φ(5) = 2·4 = 8.

(b) The powers of 2 are 2, 4, 8, 16 ≡ 1, so ord(2) = 4. Next, 4² = 16 ≡ 1, so ord(4) = 2. The powers of 7 are 7, 49 ≡ 4, 28 ≡ 13, 91 ≡ 1, so ord(7) = 4. The powers of 8 are 8, 64 ≡ 4, 32 ≡ 2, 16 ≡ 1, so ord(8) = 4. Also 11² = 121 = 8·15 + 1, so ord(11) = 2. The powers of 13 are 13, 169 ≡ 4, 52 ≡ 7, 91 ≡ 1, so ord(13) = 4. Finally 14 ≡ −1, so ord(14) = 2. Of course ord(1) = 1.

(c) A cyclic group of order 8 has an element of order 8. U(15) has none, so it is not cyclic. Let a = 2, of order 4, and b = 11, of order 2. Then ⟨a⟩ = {1, 2, 4, 8} does not contain 11, so ⟨a⟩ ∩ ⟨b⟩ = {1}. The group is abelian, so the map ℤ₄ × ℤ₂ → U(15), (i, j) ↦ 2ⁱ·11ʲ, is a homomorphism. Its kernel is trivial, since 2ⁱ = 11⁻ʲ lies in ⟨a⟩ ∩ ⟨b⟩ and so is 1, forcing i = j = 0. Both groups have 8 elements, so it is an isomorphism, and U(15) ≅ ℤ₂ × ℤ₄. This is consistent with U(15) ≅ U(3) × U(5) ≅ ℤ₂ × ℤ₄ by the CRT. Every non-identity element of ℤ₂³ has order 2, while U(15) has elements of order 4, so U(15) is not isomorphic to ℤ₂³.

(d) Since ord(7) = 4 and 101 = 4·25 + 1, 7^101 = (7⁴)²⁵·7 ≡ 7 (mod 15).

questions.q: G is a group of order 20. Which of the following cannot be the order of a subgroup of G?
questions.why: By Lagrange's theorem, the order of a subgroup divides |G| = 20, and 6 does not divide 20.

questions.q: Let H and K be subgroups of a group G. Prove that H ∩ K is a subgroup of G.
markScheme: Non-empty: e ∈ H and e ∈ K, so e ∈ H ∩ K
Takes a, b ∈ H ∩ K
ab⁻¹ ∈ H and ab⁻¹ ∈ K since each is a subgroup
So ab⁻¹ ∈ H ∩ K, and the one-step test applies
questions.modelAnswer: We use the one-step subgroup test. Both H and K contain the identity e, so H ∩ K is non-empty. Let a, b ∈ H ∩ K. Since H is a subgroup containing a and b, ab⁻¹ ∈ H. Likewise ab⁻¹ ∈ K. Hence ab⁻¹ ∈ H ∩ K, and H ∩ K ≤ G. The same argument works for the intersection of any family of subgroups. The union is a different matter: in general it is not a subgroup.

questions.q:
In S₃ (composing right to left, so στ means apply τ first), let H = {e, (1 2)}.
(a) List all the left cosets of H. [4]
(b) List all the right cosets of H. [3]
(c) Show that H is not a normal subgroup of S₃. [2]
(d) Find a subgroup N of S₃ of order 3, and explain without calculation why it is normal. [3]
markScheme: (c) (1 3)H ≠ H(1 3), so H is not normal (equivalently (1 3)(1 2)(1 3) = (2 3) ∉ H)
(d) [S₃ : N] = 2, so N is normal (or N = ker sgn)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) |S₃| = 6 and |H| = 2, so there are 3 left cosets. First, eH = (1 2)H = H = {e, (1 2)}. Next, (1 3)(1 2) sends 1 → 2 → 2, 2 → 1 → 3 and 3 → 3 → 1, so it is (1 2 3). Hence (1 3)H = {(1 3), (1 2 3)}. Similarly, (2 3)(1 2) sends 1 → 2 → 3, 3 → 3 → 2 and 2 → 1 → 1, so it is (1 3 2). Hence (2 3)H = {(2 3), (1 3 2)}. These three cosets are disjoint and cover S₃, as they must.

(b) For right cosets, (1 2)(1 3) sends 1 → 3 → 3, 3 → 1 → 2 and 2 → 2 → 1, so it is (1 3 2). Hence H(1 3) = {(1 3), (1 3 2)}. And (1 2)(2 3) sends 1 → 1 → 2, 2 → 3 → 3 and 3 → 2 → 1, so it is (1 2 3). Hence H(2 3) = {(2 3), (1 2 3)}. The third right coset is H itself.

(c) (1 3)H = {(1 3), (1 2 3)} but H(1 3) = {(1 3), (1 3 2)}. A subgroup is normal exactly when every left coset equals the corresponding right coset, so H is not normal. Equivalently, the conjugate (1 3)(1 2)(1 3)⁻¹ = (3 2) = (2 3) is not in H. This matches the conjugation rule: relabel the entries of (1 2) using (1 3).

(d) Take N = {e, (1 2 3), (1 3 2)} = A₃, of order 3. It has index 2 in S₃, so its only left cosets are N and S₃ \ N, and the same is true of its right cosets. Hence gN = Ng for all g, and N is normal. Alternatively, N is the kernel of the sign homomorphism, and kernels are always normal.

questions.q:
(a) Let H be a subgroup of a finite group G. Prove that the left cosets of H partition G into sets of size |H|, and deduce Lagrange's theorem. [7]
(b) Deduce that (i) the order of every element divides |G|, (ii) every group of prime order is cyclic, and (iii) Euler's theorem holds. [6]
(c) Prove that A₄ has no subgroup of order 6, so the converse of Lagrange's theorem fails. [7]
markScheme: (a) Defines a ~ b if and only if a⁻¹b ∈ H, and proves it is an equivalence relation whose classes are the left cosets aH
(a) The map h ↦ ah is a bijection H → aH, so every coset has |H| elements
(a) |G| = [G : H]·|H|, so |H| divides |G|
(b)(i) ord(g) = |⟨g⟩| divides |G|
(b)(ii) any g ≠ e has order p, so ⟨g⟩ = G
(b)(iii) apply (i) to a ∈ U(n), of order φ(n): a^φ(n) = 1
(c) A subgroup H of order 6 would have index 2, so it would be normal and contain the square of every element of A₄
(c) Each 3-cycle σ satisfies σ = (σ²)², so σ = (σ²)² ∈ H, which puts all 8 three-cycles in H
(c) 8 > 6 is a contradiction (alternatively, count the elements of order 2 and 3 that H must contain)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Define a ~ b if and only if a⁻¹b ∈ H. It is reflexive, since a⁻¹a = e ∈ H. It is symmetric, since if a⁻¹b ∈ H then its inverse b⁻¹a ∈ H. It is transitive, since a⁻¹b and b⁻¹c in H give their product a⁻¹c in H. The class of a is {b : a⁻¹b ∈ H} = {ah : h ∈ H} = aH. So the left cosets are equivalence classes and partition G. The map H → aH, h ↦ ah, is surjective by definition and injective by cancellation, so |aH| = |H|. If there are k = [G : H] cosets, then |G| = k|H|. Hence |H| divides |G|, which is Lagrange's theorem.

(b) (i) ⟨g⟩ is a subgroup of order ord(g), so ord(g) divides |G|, and therefore g^|G| = e. (ii) If |G| = p is prime and g ≠ e, then ord(g) divides p and is not 1, so ord(g) = p and ⟨g⟩ = G. (iii) U(n) is a group of order φ(n). For gcd(a, n) = 1, (i) gives a^φ(n) ≡ 1 (mod n). Fermat's little theorem is the case n = p.

(c) A₄ has 12 elements: the identity, the three double transpositions and eight 3-cycles. Suppose H ≤ A₄ with |H| = 6. Then [A₄ : H] = 2, so H is normal and A₄/H ≅ ℤ₂. In a group of order 2 every square is the identity, so (gH)² = H, that is g² ∈ H, for every g ∈ A₄. Take any 3-cycle σ. Then σ⁴ = σ, so σ = (σ²)², which is the square of an element and therefore lies in H. So all eight 3-cycles lie in H, but |H| = 6 < 8, a contradiction. So A₄ has no subgroup of order 6, even though 6 divides 12, and the converse of Lagrange's theorem is false.

questions.q: Let φ: GL₂(ℝ) → ℝˣ be given by φ(A) = det A. Which statement is correct?
options: ker φ = SL₂(ℝ) is a normal subgroup, and GL₂(ℝ)/SL₂(ℝ) ≅ ℝˣ
φ is injective, because det is multiplicative
ker φ is the set of scalar matrices
The image of φ is {±1}
questions.why: det is a surjective homomorphism, since diag(t, 1) has determinant t. Its kernel is the matrices of determinant 1, so the first isomorphism theorem gives the quotient ℝˣ. φ is not injective: many matrices share a determinant.

questions.q: Let φ: G → H be a group homomorphism. Prove that ker φ is a normal subgroup of G.
markScheme: φ(e) = e, so e ∈ ker φ (non-empty)
For a, b ∈ ker φ: φ(ab⁻¹) = φ(a)φ(b)⁻¹ = e, so ker φ is a subgroup
For g ∈ G and k ∈ ker φ: φ(gkg⁻¹) = φ(g)eφ(g)⁻¹ = e
So gkg⁻¹ ∈ ker φ, hence g(ker φ)g⁻¹ ⊆ ker φ and the kernel is normal
questions.modelAnswer: Since φ(e) = φ(e)φ(e), cancellation gives φ(e) = e, so e ∈ ker φ. If a, b ∈ ker φ, then φ(ab⁻¹) = φ(a)φ(b)⁻¹ = e·e = e, so ab⁻¹ ∈ ker φ, and the kernel is a subgroup. For normality, take g ∈ G and k ∈ ker φ. Then φ(gkg⁻¹) = φ(g)φ(k)φ(g)⁻¹ = φ(g)φ(g)⁻¹ = e, so gkg⁻¹ ∈ ker φ. Hence g(ker φ)g⁻¹ ⊆ ker φ for all g. Applying this with g⁻¹ gives the reverse inclusion, so the kernel is normal.

questions.q:
(a) Show that a homomorphism φ: ℤ₁₂ → ℤ₁₈ is determined by a = φ(1), and find all possible values of a. How many homomorphisms are there? [5]
(b) Show that none of them is injective. [2]
(c) For the homomorphism with φ(1) = 3, find the image and kernel, and identify ℤ₁₂/ker φ. [4]
(d) Generalise: prove that the number of homomorphisms ℤₘ → ℤₙ is gcd(m, n). [4]
markScheme: (a) φ(k) = kφ(1) = ka, by the homomorphism property
(a) Well defined: needs 12a ≡ 0 (mod 18), since 12 ≡ 0 in ℤ₁₂
(b) The image is a subgroup of ℤ₁₈ whose order divides 18, so it cannot have 12 elements (or: the order of a divides 6)
(c) ℤ₁₂/{0, 6} ≅ ℤ₆ by the first isomorphism theorem
(d) Need ma ≡ 0 (mod n), i.e. (n/d) | a where d = gcd(m, n), giving exactly d choices of a
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Since 1 generates ℤ₁₂, any homomorphism satisfies φ(k) = φ(1 + … + 1) = ka (mod 18), so φ is determined by a. Conversely, the rule k ↦ ka (mod 18) is well defined on ℤ₁₂ only if equal residues give equal images. Since 12 ≡ 0 in ℤ₁₂, we need 12a ≡ 0 (mod 18). This is also sufficient, because then k ≡ k′ (mod 12) gives ka ≡ k′a (mod 18), and the map is clearly additive. Now 18 | 12a ⇔ 3 | 2a ⇔ 3 | a, so a ∈ {0, 3, 6, 9, 12, 15}, and there are exactly 6 homomorphisms.

(b) An injective homomorphism would make im φ a subgroup of ℤ₁₈ of order 12. But 12 does not divide 18, contradicting Lagrange. More directly, each admissible a has order dividing 6 in ℤ₁₈, so the image has at most 6 elements.

(c) With a = 3, im φ = ⟨3⟩ = {0, 3, 6, 9, 12, 15}, of order 6. The kernel is {k ∈ ℤ₁₂ : 3k ≡ 0 (mod 18)} = {k : 6 | k} = {0, 6}, of order 2. This agrees with |ker|·|im| = 12. By the first isomorphism theorem, ℤ₁₂/{0, 6} ≅ ⟨3⟩, which is cyclic of order 6, so the quotient is isomorphic to ℤ₆.

(d) Let d = gcd(m, n). As in (a), homomorphisms correspond to the a ∈ ℤₙ with ma ≡ 0 (mod n). Write m = dm′ and n = dn′ with gcd(m′, n′) = 1. Then n | ma ⇔ n′ | m′a ⇔ n′ | a, by Euclid's lemma in its general form. The multiples of n′ in {0, …, n − 1} are 0, n′, …, (d − 1)n′, which is exactly d values. So there are gcd(m, n) homomorphisms. With m = 12 and n = 18 this gives 6, as found.

questions.q:
(a) Let N be a normal subgroup of G. Prove that the rule (aN)(bN) = abN gives a well-defined group operation on G/N. [6]
(b) State and prove the first isomorphism theorem. [8]
(c) Use it to show that S_n/A_n ≅ ℤ₂ for n ≥ 2, and that ℂˣ/S¹ ≅ ℝ_{>0}, where S¹ = {z : |z| = 1}. [6]
markScheme: (a) If aN = a′N and bN = b′N, then a′ = an₁ and b′ = bn₂
(a) a′b′ = ab(b⁻¹n₁b)n₂, and b⁻¹n₁b ∈ N by normality, so a′b′N = abN
(a) Group axioms: associativity inherited from G, identity eN = N, inverse a⁻¹N
(b) States G/ker φ ≅ im φ via θ(g ker φ) = φ(g)
(b) Well defined and injective: g ker φ = h ker φ ⇔ g⁻¹h ∈ ker φ ⇔ φ(g) = φ(h)
(b) θ is a homomorphism: θ(gK·hK) = φ(gh) = φ(g)φ(h); surjective onto im φ by construction
(c) sgn: S_n → {±1} is a surjective homomorphism (a transposition maps to −1) with kernel A_n, so S_n/A_n ≅ {±1} ≅ ℤ₂
(c) z ↦ |z| is a homomorphism, since |zw| = |z||w|, surjective onto ℝ_{>0} (r ↦ r), with kernel S¹
(c) Concludes ℂˣ/S¹ ≅ ℝ_{>0}
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The issue is whether the product depends on the representatives. Suppose aN = a′N and bN = b′N, so a′ = an₁ and b′ = bn₂ with n₁, n₂ ∈ N. Then a′b′ = an₁bn₂ = ab(b⁻¹n₁b)n₂. Normality gives b⁻¹n₁b ∈ N, so a′b′ ∈ abN and a′b′N = abN. Associativity is inherited from G: (aN·bN)·cN = (ab)cN = a(bc)N. The identity is eN = N, and the inverse of aN is a⁻¹N. So G/N is a group.

(b) The first isomorphism theorem says: if φ: G → H is a homomorphism with kernel K, then K ⊴ G and G/K ≅ im φ. The kernel is normal, as shown earlier, so G/K is a group by (a). Define θ: G/K → im φ by θ(gK) = φ(g). For any g, h ∈ G, gK = hK ⇔ g⁻¹h ∈ K ⇔ φ(g⁻¹h) = e ⇔ φ(g) = φ(h). Read from left to right, this says θ is well defined. Read from right to left, it says θ is injective. θ is a homomorphism, since θ(gK·hK) = θ(ghK) = φ(gh) = φ(g)φ(h) = θ(gK)θ(hK). It is surjective onto im φ by construction. So θ is an isomorphism.

(c) The sign map sgn: S_n → {±1} is a homomorphism. For n ≥ 2 it is surjective, since any transposition has sign −1. Its kernel is the set of even permutations, A_n. So S_n/A_n ≅ {±1} ≅ ℤ₂, and in particular |A_n| = n!/2. Next, define ψ: ℂˣ → ℝ_{>0} by ψ(z) = |z|. Since |zw| = |z||w|, ψ is a homomorphism from multiplication to multiplication. It is surjective, because ψ(r) = r for every r > 0. Its kernel is {z : |z| = 1} = S¹. Hence ℂˣ/S¹ ≅ ℝ_{>0}. Geometrically, each coset of S¹ is a circle centred at 0, labelled by its radius.

questions.q: What is the order of the permutation (1 2 3)(4 5) in S₅?
questions.why: For disjoint cycles, the order is the lcm of the cycle lengths: lcm(3, 2) = 6.

questions.q: The permutation σ ∈ S₈ sends 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 to 3, 5, 1, 8, 7, 2, 4, 6 respectively. Write σ as a product of disjoint cycles, and find its order and sign. Is σ ∈ A₈?
markScheme: Order lcm(2, 6) = 6
Sign (−1)¹(−1)⁵ = +1, so σ is even and lies in A₈
questions.modelAnswer: Following 1: 1 → 3 → 1, which gives the cycle (1 3). Following 2: 2 → 5 → 7 → 4 → 8 → 6 → 2, which gives the 6-cycle (2 5 7 4 8 6). Every point is now accounted for, so σ = (1 3)(2 5 7 4 8 6). Its order is lcm(2, 6) = 6. A k-cycle has sign (−1)^(k−1), so sgn σ = (−1)¹ × (−1)⁵ = +1. As a check, (−1)^(8 − 2) = +1, since there are two cycles. So σ is even, and σ ∈ A₈.

questions.q: Prove that for any τ ∈ S_n and any k-cycle (a₁ a₂ … a_k), τ(a₁ a₂ … a_k)τ⁻¹ = (τ(a₁) τ(a₂) … τ(a_k)). Deduce that permutations with the same cycle type are conjugate.
markScheme: Evaluates the left side at τ(aᵢ): τ⁻¹ gives aᵢ, the cycle gives aᵢ₊₁, and τ gives τ(aᵢ₊₁) (indices mod k)
For x not of the form τ(aᵢ): τ⁻¹(x) is not among the aᵢ, so it is fixed by the cycle, and x is fixed overall
Both sides agree on every point, so they are equal
Deduction: given two permutations with the same cycle type, line up the cycles and let τ send each entry to the matching entry; then τστ⁻¹ = σ′ cycle by cycle
questions.modelAnswer: Let c = (a₁ … a_k) and evaluate τcτ⁻¹ at each point. At τ(aᵢ), τ⁻¹ gives aᵢ, then c gives aᵢ₊₁ (with a_{k+1} = a₁), then τ gives τ(aᵢ₊₁). So τ(aᵢ) ↦ τ(aᵢ₊₁). If x is not one of the τ(aᵢ), then τ⁻¹(x) is not an aᵢ, so c fixes it and x ↦ x. This is exactly the action of (τ(a₁) … τ(a_k)). For the deduction, write σ and σ′ as disjoint cycles of the same lengths, including 1-cycles, aligned one above the other. Let τ send each entry of σ to the entry in the same position of σ′. Applying the formula to each cycle gives τστ⁻¹ = σ′.

questions.q:
In S₆, composing right to left (στ means apply τ first), let σ = (1 2 3)(4 5) and τ = (1 4)(2 6 3).
(a) Compute στ and τσ as products of disjoint cycles. [4]
(b) Find the order and sign of σ, τ, στ and τσ. [4]
(c) Compute τστ⁻¹, and explain how to obtain it without composing. [2]
(d) Are στ and τσ conjugate in S₆? Justify your answer. [2]
markScheme: (b) σ has order 6 and sign (+1)(−1) = −1
(b) τ has order 6 and sign (−1)(+1) = −1
(b) στ and τσ are 5-cycles, each of order 5 and sign +1 (consistent with sgn(στ) = sgn σ·sgn τ = +1)
(c) Relabel each entry of σ by τ
(d) Yes: same cycle type (a 5-cycle), and indeed τσ = τ(στ)τ⁻¹
questions.modelAnswer:
First record the maps. σ sends 1 → 2, 2 → 3, 3 → 1, 4 → 5, 5 → 4 and fixes 6. τ sends 1 → 4, 4 → 1, 2 → 6, 6 → 3, 3 → 2 and fixes 5.

(a) For στ, apply τ then σ: 1 → 4 → 5, 5 → 5 → 4, 4 → 1 → 2, 2 → 6 → 6, 6 → 3 → 1, and 3 → 2 → 3. So στ = (1 5 4 2 6), with 3 fixed. For τσ, apply σ then τ: 1 → 2 → 6, 6 → 6 → 3, 3 → 1 → 4, 4 → 5 → 5, 5 → 4 → 1, and 2 → 3 → 2. So τσ = (1 6 3 4 5), with 2 fixed. Note that στ ≠ τσ, so σ and τ do not commute.

(b) σ has cycle type (3, 2), so its order is lcm(3, 2) = 6 and its sign is (+1)(−1) = −1. τ also has cycle type (2, 3), so it too has order 6 and sign −1. Both στ and τσ are 5-cycles, so each has order 5 and sign (−1)⁴ = +1. This is consistent with sgn being a homomorphism: sgn(στ) = (−1)(−1) = +1.

(c) By the conjugation formula, τστ⁻¹ is obtained by applying τ to every entry in the cycles of σ: τστ⁻¹ = (τ(1) τ(2) τ(3))(τ(4) τ(5)) = (4 6 2)(1 5) = (1 5)(2 4 6). It has the same cycle type as σ, as it must.

(d) Yes. Two permutations in S_n are conjugate exactly when they have the same cycle type, and στ and τσ are both 5-cycles. More directly, τσ = τ(στ)τ⁻¹ in any group, so XY and YX are always conjugate. Checking with the formula, τ(1 5 4 2 6)τ⁻¹ = (4 5 1 6 3) = (1 6 3 4 5), as found in (a).

questions.q:
(a) Prove that every permutation in S_n is a product of transpositions. You may assume the disjoint cycle decomposition. [4]
(b) State and prove Cayley's theorem. [6]
(c) List the cycle types in S₅, with the size of each conjugacy class, and check that the sizes sum to |S₅|. [6]
(d) Prove that A_n is generated by 3-cycles for n ≥ 3. [4]
markScheme: (a) (a₁ … a_k) = (a₁ a_k)(a₁ a_{k−1})⋯(a₁ a₂), verified on the points, so each cycle and hence each permutation is a product of transpositions
(b) Statement: every group G is isomorphic to a subgroup of Sym(G)
(b) λ_g(x) = gx is a bijection of G, with inverse λ_{g⁻¹}
(b) λ_{gh} = λ_g ∘ λ_h, so g ↦ λ_g is a homomorphism, injective since λ_g = id ⇒ g = ge = e
(c) Types and class sizes: e 1; (2) 10; (3) 20; (4) 30; (5) 24
(c) (2, 2) 15; (3, 2) 20; total 120, with class-size formulas such as 5!/(4·1) = 30
(d) Each even permutation is a product of an even number of transpositions, grouped in pairs
(d) (a b)(a c) = (a c b) and (a b)(c d) = (a c b)(a c d) for distinct a, b, c, d, so each pair is a product of 3-cycles; 3-cycles are even, so they lie in A_n
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Every permutation is a product of disjoint cycles, so it is enough to treat a single cycle. Composing right to left, (a₁ a₂ … a_k) = (a₁ a_k)(a₁ a_{k−1})⋯(a₁ a₂). Check: a₁ is sent to a₂ by the first factor applied, (a₁ a₂), and then fixed. For 2 ≤ i < k, aᵢ is fixed by the factors (a₁ aⱼ) with j < i, sent to a₁ by (a₁ aᵢ), then to aᵢ₊₁ by (a₁ aᵢ₊₁), and fixed by the rest. Finally a_k is fixed until the last factor (a₁ a_k) sends it to a₁. The identity is the empty product, or (1 2)(1 2).

(b) Cayley's theorem: every group G is isomorphic to a subgroup of Sym(G), so every group of order n embeds in S_n. For g ∈ G, define λ_g: G → G by λ_g(x) = gx. It is a bijection with inverse λ_{g⁻¹}. Since λ_{gh}(x) = ghx = λ_g(λ_h(x)), the map g ↦ λ_g is a homomorphism G → Sym(G). It is injective, because λ_g = id gives g = ge = e. So G is isomorphic to its image, a subgroup of Sym(G).

(c) A class with cycle type having mᵢ cycles of length i has size n!/Π(i^mᵢ mᵢ!). For S₅: the identity 1; transpositions 10; 3-cycles 20; 4-cycles 120/4 = 30; 5-cycles 120/5 = 24; double transpositions 120/(2²·2!) = 15; a 3-cycle with a disjoint 2-cycle 120/(3·2) = 20. Total: 1 + 10 + 20 + 30 + 24 + 15 + 20 = 120 = 5!.

(d) A 3-cycle is a product of two transpositions, so it is even, and the 3-cycles generate a subgroup of A_n. Conversely, by (a) and the well-definedness of sign, an even permutation is a product of an even number of transpositions. Group them in consecutive pairs. If the two transpositions in a pair are equal, the pair is the identity. If they share one point, (a b)(a c) = (a c b). If they are disjoint, (a b)(c d) = (a b)(b c)(b c)(c d) = (b c a)(c d b), a product of two 3-cycles. So every even permutation is a product of 3-cycles.

questions.q: Which of the following rings is a field?
options: ℤ₇
ℤ₈
ℤ
ℤ₆
questions.why: ℤₙ is a field exactly when n is prime, so ℤ₇ is a field. ℤ₈ and ℤ₆ have zero divisors (2·4 = 0 and 2·3 = 0), and ℤ lacks inverses for elements such as 2.

questions.q: Consider f(x) = x⁴ + x² + 1 over F₂. Which statement is true?
options: f has no roots in F₂ but is reducible, since f = (x² + x + 1)²
f has no roots in F₂, so it is irreducible
f has the root x = 1, so it is reducible
f is irreducible by Eisenstein's criterion
questions.why: f(0) = 1 and f(1) = 3 ≡ 1, so f has no roots. But in characteristic 2, (x² + x + 1)² = x⁴ + x² + 1. The 'no roots' test detects irreducibility only in degrees 2 and 3.

questions.q: Prove that every finite integral domain is a field.
markScheme: Takes a ≠ 0 and defines m_a: R → R, x ↦ ax
m_a is injective: ax = ay ⇒ a(x − y) = 0 ⇒ x = y, since there are no zero divisors
Injective self-map of a finite set is surjective
So ax = 1 for some x, and a is a unit
R is commutative with 1 ≠ 0 (integral domain), so R is a field
questions.modelAnswer: Let R be a finite integral domain and a ≠ 0 in R. Define m_a: R → R by m_a(x) = ax. If ax = ay, then a(x − y) = 0, and since R has no zero divisors and a ≠ 0, x = y. So m_a is injective. An injective map from a finite set to itself is surjective, so there is some x with ax = 1. Every non-zero element is therefore a unit. Since R is commutative with 1 ≠ 0, it is a field. In particular ℤₚ is a field for p prime.

questions.q:
Let F = F₂[x]/(x³ + x + 1), and let α denote the class of x, so that α³ + α + 1 = 0.
(a) Prove that x³ + x + 1 is irreducible over F₂, and deduce that F is a field. How many elements does it have? [4]
(b) Express α³, α⁴, α⁵, α⁶ and α⁷ in the form a + bα + cα², with a, b, c ∈ F₂. [4]
(c) Deduce that the multiplicative group Fˣ is cyclic, and explain why every non-identity element generates it. [3]
(d) Find α⁻¹ and (α²)⁻¹. [3]
markScheme: (a) Values at 0 and 1 are both 1, so there are no roots; a reducible cubic must have a linear factor, so it is irreducible
(a) F₂[x]/(p) is a field when p is irreducible; it has 2³ = 8 elements
(b) α³ = α + 1 (signs do not matter in characteristic 2)
(b) α⁴ = α² + α and α⁵ = α³ + α² = α² + α + 1
(b) α⁶ = α³ + α² + α = α² + 1, and α⁷ = α³ + α = 1
(c) The powers α⁰, …, α⁶ are the 7 distinct non-zero elements, so α generates Fˣ ≅ ℤ₇
(c) 7 is prime, so every non-identity element has order 7 by Lagrange
(d) α⁻¹ = α⁶ = α² + 1 and (α²)⁻¹ = α⁵ = α² + α + 1, with verification
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Let p(x) = x³ + x + 1. Then p(0) = 1 and p(1) = 1 + 1 + 1 = 1 in F₂, so p has no root in F₂. If a cubic factored, one factor would be linear and would give a root. So p is irreducible. For a field K, K[x]/(p) is a field exactly when p is irreducible, because (p) is then a maximal ideal. So F is a field. Its elements are the remainders a + bα + cα² with a, b, c ∈ F₂, so |F| = 2³ = 8.

(b) From α³ + α + 1 = 0 and −1 = 1 in F₂, α³ = α + 1. Then α⁴ = α·α³ = α² + α. Next, α⁵ = α³ + α² = α² + α + 1. Then α⁶ = α³ + α² + α = (α + 1) + α² + α = α² + 1. Finally α⁷ = α³ + α = (α + 1) + α = 1.

(c) The seven powers 1, α, α², α + 1, α² + α, α² + α + 1, α² + 1 are distinct, and they are all the non-zero elements of F. So α has order 7, and Fˣ = ⟨α⟩ is cyclic of order 7, isomorphic to ℤ₇. Since 7 is prime, Lagrange's theorem forces every element other than 1 to have order 7, so each one generates Fˣ. This illustrates the general theorem that the multiplicative group of any finite field is cyclic.

(d) Since α⁷ = 1, α⁻¹ = α⁶ = α² + 1. Check: α(α² + 1) = α³ + α = (α + 1) + α = 1. Similarly (α²)⁻¹ = α⁵ = α² + α + 1. Check: α²·α⁵ = α⁷ = 1.

questions.q:
Let R be a commutative ring with 1, and let I be an ideal with I ≠ R.
(a) Prove that I is maximal if and only if R/I is a field. [7]
(b) Prove that I is prime if and only if R/I is an integral domain, and deduce that every maximal ideal is prime. [5]
(c) Show that in ℤ the ideal (n), for n ≥ 2, is maximal if and only if n is prime. [3]
(d) Show that in ℤ[x] the ideal (x) is prime but not maximal, and give a maximal ideal containing it. [5]
markScheme: (a) (⇒) For a ∉ I, the ideal I + Ra strictly contains I, so it equals R; then 1 = i + ra, giving (r + I)(a + I) = 1 + I
(a) (⇐) If J ⊋ I is an ideal and a ∈ J \ I, then a + I has an inverse b + I, so 1 − ab ∈ I ⊆ J, and 1 ∈ J, so J = R
(a) Notes that 1 ≠ 0 in R/I because I ≠ R
(b) ab ∈ I ⇒ a ∈ I or b ∈ I translates to (a + I)(b + I) = 0 ⇒ a + I = 0 or b + I = 0
(b) Fields are integral domains, so maximal ideals are prime
(c) ℤ/(n) ≅ ℤₙ, which is a field if and only if n is prime
(d) ℤ[x]/(x) ≅ ℤ via evaluation f ↦ f(0) and the first isomorphism theorem for rings
(d) ℤ is an integral domain but not a field, so (x) is prime but not maximal
(d) (2, x) ⊋ (x), and ℤ[x]/(2, x) ≅ F₂ is a field, so (2, x) is maximal
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) (⇒) Suppose I is maximal and a + I ≠ 0, that is a ∉ I. Then J = I + Ra = {i + ra} is an ideal strictly containing I, so J = R by maximality. Hence 1 = i + ra for some i ∈ I and r ∈ R, which gives (r + I)(a + I) = 1 + I. So every non-zero element of R/I is invertible. Since 1 ∉ I, 1 + I ≠ 0, so R/I is a field. (⇐) Suppose R/I is a field and J is an ideal with I ⊊ J. Pick a ∈ J \ I. Then a + I has an inverse b + I, so 1 − ab ∈ I ⊆ J. Since ab ∈ J, it follows that 1 ∈ J and J = R. So I is maximal.

(b) By definition, I ≠ R is prime if ab ∈ I implies a ∈ I or b ∈ I. In R/I this reads: (a + I)(b + I) = 0 implies a + I = 0 or b + I = 0. Together with 1 + I ≠ 0, this is exactly the statement that R/I is an integral domain. Every field is an integral domain, so by (a) every maximal ideal is prime.

(c) ℤ/(n) ≅ ℤₙ, so by (a), (n) is maximal exactly when ℤₙ is a field, that is, when n is prime. If n = ab with 1 < a, b < n, then [a][b] = 0.

(d) The evaluation map ev₀: ℤ[x] → ℤ, f ↦ f(0), is a surjective ring homomorphism whose kernel is the set of polynomials with zero constant term, namely (x). So ℤ[x]/(x) ≅ ℤ. Since ℤ is an integral domain but not a field, (x) is prime but not maximal by (a) and (b). It lies strictly inside (2, x), the polynomials with even constant term. Reducing f(0) modulo 2 gives a surjection ℤ[x] → F₂ with kernel (2, x), so ℤ[x]/(2, x) ≅ F₂ is a field and (2, x) is maximal.
